sources.title: Electric vehicle charging infrastructure statistics collection
Public electric vehicle charging infrastructure statistics: 1 April 2026
Smart meters in Great Britain, quarterly update March 2026
Great Britain Fuel Mix Disclosure 2026: REGOs
Farm Practices Survey: manure and slurry storage

guard_patterns.handling: Require directly accessible official public source.
Keep measurements, administrative counts, survey responses and infrastructure counts distinct.
Preserve month, quarter, disclosure year and survey date.
Preserve GB, UK, England/Wales, England and local-authority scopes.
Retain official/in-development status and definition changes.
Keep heat pumps, biomass, meters, chargers and farm practices distinct.
Retain scheme eligibility, supplier coverage and survey-sample limits.
Do not convert uptake, stock or practice prevalence directly to GHG.
No parcel emissions without geometry, identity, activity and method binding.
Every fact/guard combination must pass deterministic scope review.

packages.title: Ofgem BUS cumulative uptake QA
facts: Ofgem updated the BUS monthly scheme page on 10 July 2026.
The reporting period runs from scheme start through 30 June 2026.
Voucher applications received are counted separately from vouchers issued.
Voucher redemptions are counted separately from vouchers issued.
Grant payments are reported separately from voucher face value.
The page reports annual scheme-budget spending.
Expired, revoked or withdrawn vouchers are excluded from the issued-voucher figure note.
Rejected, revoked or withdrawn redemption applications are excluded from the redemption-application note.
Scheme uptake is administrative activity rather than measured building GHG.
Parcel emissions require a separate building and energy-use binding step.

packages.title: BUS voucher versus installation guard QA
facts: BUS statistics track applications, vouchers and redemptions as distinct stages.
A voucher application is not an installed technology.
A voucher issued is not automatically a redeemed voucher.
A redeemed voucher supports a completed grant process but is not a continuous emissions measurement.
BUS statistics include installation-cost information.
DESNZ publishes the scheme statistics for England and Wales.
Technology uptake can support low-carbon-heat screening.
Administrative scheme counts should retain their reference month.
Scheme participation does not establish actual annual heat demand.
Parcel-level GHG remains unbound without property identity and metered/activity data.

packages.title: BUS technology-scope guard QA
facts: BUS monitoring includes air-source heat pumps.
BUS monitoring includes ground-source heat pumps.
BUS monitoring includes biomass boilers under scheme rules.
Technology categories must remain separate.
A heat-pump installation does not by itself state electricity consumed.
A biomass installation does not by itself state fuel consumed.
Technology type is evidence for candidate building-energy context.
Technology deployment is not a direct CO2e observation.
Scheme geography is broader than a cadastral parcel.
Parcel emissions need verified property and activity linkage.

packages.title: DfT EV charger definition-change QA
facts: DfT changed the statistical focus from charging devices to chargers from January 2026.
The newer charger measure represents vehicles that can charge.
The change is intended to better represent public charging infrastructure.
Historic device measures remain a different concept.
Series comparisons must preserve the definition change.
The quarterly release uses charger data reported by charge-point operators.
Zapmap collates the data for DfT.
Operational status is reported at the statistical snapshot time.
Charger counts are infrastructure counts rather than vehicle-energy consumption.
Infrastructure counts cannot be converted directly into parcel GHG.

packages.title: DfT EV charger operational-snapshot QA
facts: The 1 April 2026 release is an official statistics publication.
The data are correct as of 1 April 2026.
The UK total was 119,080 public EV chargers.
Of these, 27,372 were rated rapid or above at 50 kW or higher.
The statistics cover publicly available infrastructure.
The data source is charge-point operators via Zapmap.
The next quarterly report was scheduled for August 2026.
A charger snapshot is not a utilisation measurement.
Rated charging power is not energy delivered over a period.
Parcel emissions require charger identity plus actual energy/activity evidence.

packages.title: ONS EV charger geography/rate guard QA
facts: ONS publishes public EV charger indicators as official statistics in development.
The indicator can be shown per 100,000 population.
The local geography includes lower-tier and unitary authorities.
The displayed data cover quarterly snapshots.
The source is DfT data sourced from Zapmap.
The measure reports chargers operational at the quarter-start snapshot.
Local charger counts can decrease between publications.
A local decrease can reflect reporting changes or operational status as well as physical removal.
Population-normalised charger rates are not electricity-use rates.
Local authority infrastructure indicators are not parcel GHG measurements.

packages.title: EV charging infrastructure versus use-emissions QA
facts: Public charging statistics describe infrastructure availability.
They do not measure kilometres driven by electric vehicles.
They do not measure electricity delivered by every charger.
They do not provide vehicle lifecycle emissions.
They do not provide site electricity-generation mix.
Rapid-charger counts are capacity context, not GHG totals.
Local charger density can support transport-transition context.
Use-phase emissions need energy consumption and compatible electricity factors.
A charger location still requires parcel-geometry verification.
No parcel CO2e is inferred from charger presence alone.

packages.title: DESNZ smart-meter operating versus installed QA
facts: DESNZ published the March 2026 quarterly smart-meter update on 28 May 2026.
The release covers January to March 2026 installations by large suppliers.
It separately reports meters operating at the end of March 2026.
Smart and non-smart meters are distinct categories.
Installed and operating-in-smart-mode concepts are distinct.
The series extends back to 2012.
The publication applies to England, Scotland and Wales.
Meter deployment can support data-availability context.
A smart meter does not itself disclose gas or electricity consumption in this publication.
Parcel GHG requires actual consumption and verified meter/property binding.

packages.title: DESNZ smart-meter supplier/time-base QA
facts: Quarterly smart-meter statistics update large-supplier data each quarter.
The collection includes domestic smart meters.
It also includes smart and advanced meters at smaller non-domestic sites.
Whole-market small-supplier information follows a different annual timing in the series.
Quarterly and annual coverage should not be silently mixed.
Operating meters and newly installed meters have different reference concepts.
Supplier coverage is part of provenance.
Meter counts are administrative infrastructure statistics.
Meter counts do not establish energy demand.
Parcel emissions remain null without consumption records and property identity.

packages.title: Smart-meter local-authority estimate guard QA
facts: The smart-meter statistical series includes local-authority context for domestic electricity smart-meter uptake in its reporting framework.
Local-authority estimates are broader than individual properties.
An uptake percentage does not identify a specific meter.
A smart-meter percentage does not quantify electricity consumed.
Local-authority boundaries do not equal parcel boundaries.
Coverage assumptions should be retained with derived local indicators.
Quarter-end timing matters for uptake comparisons.
Infrastructure adoption can improve candidate confidence for data availability.
It cannot establish building operational emissions by itself.
Property-level use requires verified meter and address/geometry binding.

packages.title: Ofgem Fuel Mix Disclosure period QA
facts: Fuel Mix Disclosure applies annually to Great Britain electricity suppliers.
The disclosure period runs from 1 April to 31 March.
Suppliers disclose the fuel mix used to generate electricity supplied to customers.
The disclosure obligation applies where supply spans the full disclosure period under the rules.
Fuel-mix reporting is an electricity-supplier disclosure process.
The reporting period must be preserved when comparing suppliers.
Supplier fuel mix is not the same as real-time grid mix at a property.
Supplier disclosure is not metered building consumption.
FMD can support electricity-factor provenance.
Parcel GHG requires consumption plus a compatible factor and property binding.

packages.title: Ofgem FMD REGO evidence guard QA
facts: Ofgem published GB Fuel Mix Disclosure 2026 REGO guidance on 18 May 2026.
The guidance applies to electricity suppliers and generators using the Renewable Electricity Register.
REGOs support renewable-electricity evidence for FMD.
REGOs for the disclosure period must be held by the relevant July deadline under the FMD process.
Ofgem redeems eligible REGOs to capture their use for GB FMD.
EU Guarantees of Origin are no longer recognised for GB FMD from the disclosure period beginning 1 April 2023.
Non-EU GoOs are not recognised for GB FMD.
Certificates are evidence instruments rather than physical electricity flows to one parcel.
Supplier-level renewable evidence does not quantify site consumption.
Parcel emissions require consumption, factor version and identity binding.

packages.title: Supplier fuel mix versus parcel-emissions QA
facts: FMD provides supplier-level fuel-source transparency.
A supplier can serve many properties across Great Britain.
A parcel can change supplier across reporting periods.
Supplier fuel mix is annual rather than a property interval-load profile.
Renewable evidence certificates do not prove a particular electron path to a building.
FMD is useful for supplier-reporting provenance.
FMD should not replace actual meter consumption.
FMD should not be treated as a parcel boundary dataset.
Any emissions calculation needs an explicitly selected factor methodology.
No parcel CO2e is produced without consumption and parcel binding.

packages.title: Defra Farm Practices Survey sample-scope QA
facts: The February 2026 Farm Practices Survey applies to England.
The survey is run annually.
Approximately 7,000 holdings were sent the 2026 survey questions.
Topics include nutrient and manure management.
Topics include anaerobic digestion.
Topics include emissions actions.
Topics include fertiliser and slurry spreading and storage.
Survey percentages describe responding/sample-based holding populations rather than every parcel.
Survey prevalence is not a direct GHG measurement.
Parcel attribution requires farm/holding and field geometry plus activity evidence.

packages.title: Defra farm GHG-action self-report QA
facts: The 2026 survey reports that 47% of farmers were taking action to reduce farm GHG emissions.
Recycling farm waste was one of the most common reported actions.
Improving energy efficiency was one of the most common reported actions.
Reducing tillage or using no-tillage was reported.
Improving nitrogen-fertiliser application accuracy was reported.
Increasing clover use in grassland was reported.
Improving manure/slurry management efficiency was reported.
Methane-suppressing feed products were regularly used by a small minority of farms in the survey.
Self-reported practice adoption does not quantify tonnes of CO2e avoided.
Parcel GHG cannot be inferred from practice prevalence alone.

packages.title: Defra nutrient-management plan QA
facts: Effective nutrient management is described as helping manage environmental impacts.
It can help minimise GHG emissions while meeting crop and grassland nutrient needs.
In 2026, 69% of holdings reported a nutrient-management plan in the survey headline.
Approximately 73% of farms reported a manure-management plan.
Most farms with a manure-management plan used RB209 or CoGAP as a recommendation source.
Management-plan presence is a practice indicator.
A plan does not state actual nitrogen applied to each field.
A plan does not directly quantify N2O emissions.
Holding-level survey results are broader than individual parcel values.
Parcel GHG needs field activity, method and geometry evidence.

packages.title: Defra soil-organic-matter monitoring QA
facts: The Farm Practices Survey asks about monitoring soil organic matter.
In 2026, 65% of farmers reported keeping track of soil organic matter.
The reported proportion increased from 59% in 2025.
Soil organic matter is relevant to nutrient and water retention.
Survey monitoring status does not provide measured soil-carbon stock values.
Monitoring does not establish sequestration rate.
A farm-level response does not identify every field sampled.
Soil-carbon inference requires sampling and method details.
Parcel boundaries are not supplied by the survey result.
No parcel sequestration or GHG value is inferred from monitoring prevalence.

packages.title: Defra anaerobic-digestion uptake QA
facts: Anaerobic digestion breaks down plant and animal materials without oxygen.
The process produces biogas that can be used for electricity and heat.
Digestate remains nutrient-rich and can be used as fertiliser.
The survey reports 15% of farms processing waste, crops or feedstocks by anaerobic digestion in 2026.
The comparable 2022 survey figure was 8%.
AD uptake has increased across recent survey years.
AD can improve capture and treatment of nutrients and GHG from slurries/manures relative to direct spreading contexts.
AD presence does not quantify methane capture efficiency at a specific plant.
Farm survey uptake does not identify exact digester geometry.
Parcel GHG requires installation, feedstock, energy and geometry binding.

packages.title: Defra anaerobic-digestion feedstock-scope QA
facts: The 2026 survey distinguishes crops including silage as an AD material category.
It distinguishes slurries and manures.
It distinguishes other feedstocks.
Crops including silage were the most commonly reported AD material category in the survey.
Slurries/manures were another reported material category.
Feedstock category affects process context.
Feedstock prevalence does not provide tonnes processed.
Feedstock category does not provide methane yield.
Farm-level survey reporting is not a facility emissions inventory.
Parcel GHG needs facility-specific throughput and process evidence.

packages.title: Defra manure/slurry storage activity guard QA
facts: Manure and slurry management is relevant to environmental risks to water and air.
Good management can reduce ammonia losses and retain nitrogen for fertiliser use.
The 2026 survey reports open field storage without cover as a common manure-storage method.
Above-ground tanks without cover were a common slurry-storage method in the survey.
Storage-method prevalence is a management-practice indicator.
It does not state storage duration for each holding.
It does not provide measured methane or N2O flux.
Survey percentages do not identify a particular storage structure.
Emission estimation requires activity and method-specific factors or measurements.
Parcel GHG remains unbound without storage-site geometry and activity evidence.

packages.title: Farm-practice precision and interpretation guard QA
facts: Farm Practices Survey results are sample-based official statistics for England.
Survey questions cover multiple environmental practices.
Reported percentages are prevalence estimates, not universal farm facts.
A practice can reduce emissions without the survey quantifying the reduction magnitude.
A practice can be reported without continuous monitoring.
Holding-level reporting can cover multiple land parcels.
Practice adoption dates may differ within the reference year.
Methodology and sample scope must accompany downstream use.
Candidate scoring can use practice evidence qualitatively.
Numeric parcel CO2e must not be generated from prevalence alone.

packages.title: Cross-source heat/meter/EV/farm parcel-binding guard QA
facts: BUS data describe scheme uptake and grants.
Smart-meter statistics describe meter infrastructure and operating status.
EV-charging statistics describe public charging infrastructure.
Fuel Mix Disclosure describes supplier-level annual electricity provenance.
Farm Practices Survey describes sample-based management-practice prevalence.
These sources operate at different geographies and reference periods.
None alone provides a cadastral parcel GHG measurement.
Combining them can strengthen contextual candidate evidence.
A valid parcel estimate still requires parcel geometry, source/property identity, activity data and compatible methodology.
Until those bindings exist, measured parcel emissions remain null.
